chunks: Increasing CPU throughput. The question: What can you do to increase the throughput of a CPU?
Program run time equals the number of instructions, times the average clock cycles per instruction (CPI), times the length of one clock cycle.
Every way of making a CPU faster attacks one of those three.
You can shorten the cycle, keep the hardware busy so each instruction needs fewer cycles, or make each instruction do more work.
Picture a bakery making 1,000 rolls. Total time is rolls times minutes per roll. A bigger tray lets one action handle several rolls, which is fewer instructions.
Keeping every oven and worker busy is a lower CPI. A hotter oven is a faster clock, but it burns much more fuel.
The slowest part is often waiting for flour to arrive, like a CPU waiting on memory.
Every percentage point of miss rate costs 0. 3 CPI in this model.
Going from a 5% to 2% miss rate (bigger or better-organized cache, prefetching, blocking in the code) speeds the program up by 2. 5/1. 6 = 1.
56x, far more than any ALU improvement could, because the core was idle waiting on memory 60% of the time at 5%.
Instruction count: how many instructions the program needs. CPI: average clock cycles per instruction.
Its inverse is IPC, instructions per cycle ("Characterizing CPU performance"). Clock period: the time of one cycle, which is 1 divided by the clock frequency.
Cache miss: the data wanted isn't in the small fast memory, so the CPU waits for slow main memory.
Say the ideal CPI is 1, but 30% of instructions access memory, 5% of those accesses miss the cache, and each miss costs 100 cycles. Then CPI = 1 plus 0. 3 times 0.
05 times 100 equals 2. 5 . The CPU is idle more than half the time, waiting on memory. Cut the miss rate to 2% and CPI becomes 1 plus 0. 3 times 0. 02 times 100 equals 1. 6 .
That is 2. 5 / 1. 6, about 1. 56 times faster, with no change to the clock. That is the whole idea: find which factor is the bottleneck.
"I'd use the iron law: time is instruction count times CPI times clock period. To cut the clock period, make stages shorter, with a power cost.
To cut CPI, use pipelining, superscalar and out-of-order execution, branch prediction and caches so the CPU is never waiting.
To cut instruction count, use better compilers and SIMD. Beyond that, add parallelism with multithreading, multiple cores and accelerators.
The limits are power, memory bandwidth and Amdahl's law."
